name: Thavung
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.

new_statements.quote: The phonological word in So (T) may consist of one, two, or three syllables. Disyllabic words are most frequent and trisyllabic words are rare. Like other Mon-Khmer languages, the stress is always on the main syllable which is the last syllable of the word. The presyllable always gets the reduced stress and transitional vowel. [...] (4.1.2) The stressed main syllable has the full vowel quality, whereas the unstressed presyllable has the reduced vowel. [...] (p. xiii) It is also quite obvious that when a word does not occur in the final position of the utterence its pitch is neutral.
new_statements.citation: Suwilai Premsrirat. 2000. So (Thavung) preliminary dictionary. Institute of Language and Culture for Rural Development, Mahidol University.
new_statements.locator: Introduction, section 4.1.1 'Basic structure', printed p. iv (scan page 9); also 4.1.2 p. iv and 4.2.3.2 'Pitch in So (T)' pp. xii-xiii (scan pp. 17-18)

Disyllabic words are most frequent and trisyllabic words are rare. Like other Mon-Khmer languages, the stress is a…
new_statements.relation_note: Catalog 'fixed-dominant final stress (final stress in di- and trisyllables) is exactly what p. iv states, including the trisyllabic template Cv(C)Cv'(CV(C). Same author as the catalog's the deciding source (Suwilai 1996 MKS 26 p.166) and same So (Thavung) variety of Sakon Nakhon, so this is a restatement rather than an independent witness; it adds the sesquisyllabic word templates and the register/pitch description (pp. x-xiii).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are mono-, di- or (rarely) tri-syllabic; stress always falls on the main syllable, which is the last syllable of the word ('(CV(C), Cv(C)'(CV(C), Cv(C)Cv'(CV(C)); presyllables carry reduced stress and a reduced/transitional vowel and may be dropped. The main syllable additionally carries a register complex (clear / tense-creaky / lax-breathy voice) with associated pitches (rising, high-falling, mid-level, mid-falling), partly contrastive and described as an incipient Thai-Lao-type tone system; word pitch is neutralised when the word is not utterance-final.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; presyllables are said to get 'reduced stress' (i.e. unstressed, reduced vowel).
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement. Variation concerns presyllable deletion (disyllable ~ monosyllable variants) and vowel/register variation across age groups; pitch contrasts neutralised in non-final utterance position (p. xiii).
new_statements.identity_note: Suwilai 2000 describes 'So (Thavung)' = So (T) as spoken in Ban Nongwaeng and the adjacent villages Ban Nongjaroen and Ban Nongmuang, Songdao district, Sakon Nakhon province, NE Thailand (c. 1,000 speakers; data pooled from elderly, middle-aged and young speakers of a language in transition toward Thai-Lao). Srisakorn 2008 treats the same community (Nong Waeng and Nong Muang villages, Pathum Wapi subdistrict, Song Dao district, Sakon Nakhon; fieldwork 2005-2007; c. 100 fluent speakers). The Thavung/Phon Soung varieties of Khamkeut, Bolikhamxai, Laos (Ferlus 1979; Waiyanont 1998) are the Lao side of the same glottocode.

tone_statements.citation: Ferlus, Michel. 1999. Les disharmonies tonales en viet-muong et leurs implications historiques. Cahiers de Linguistique Asie Orientale 28(1): 83-99. doi:10.3406/clao.1999.1546 (author-revised 2015 version: HAL halshs-01135816, pp. given as 83-100)
tone_statements.quote: Toutes les langues du groupe vietique sont des langues tonales. Le ton se manifeste sur la voyelle de la syllabe principale du mot ... Le nombre des tons contrastifs peut aller de six (vietnamien, mường, cuối) à quatre (pong, sách/rục, thavung) quelle que soit la raison de cette réduction. ... Dans certaines langues vietiques minoritaires le système de base peut se réduire à 4 (+2) tons, soit parce que l’ancien -h final est préservé à la place des tons a⁵-a⁶ (mãliềng, arem, sách/rục, thavung)
tone_statements.translation: All the languages of the Vietic group are tone languages. Tone is realised on the vowel of the main syllable of the word ... The number of contrastive tones ranges from six (Vietnamese, Muong, Cuoi) to four (Pong, Sach/Ruc, Thavung), whatever the reason for this reduction. ... In some minority Vietic languages the basic system may reduce to 4 (+2) tones, either because the old final -h is preserved in place of tones a5-a6 (Malieng, Arem, Sach/Ruc, Thavung)
tone_statements.locator: Introduction, HAL version p. 1 (= CLAO 28(1) p. 83) and p. 2
tone_statements.summary: Four contrastive tones (4 (+2): two more on stop-final syllables), etymological categories 1-4, 7-8; old -h kept instead of tones 5-6; one tone per word on the main syllable; no phonetic values given.

tone_statements.citation: Ferlus, Michel. 1998. Les systèmes de tons dans les langues viet-muong. Diachronica 15(1): 1-27. doi:10.1075/dia.15.1.02fer
tone_statements.quote: Le sách/rục et le thavung ont un système à quatre tons avec des voyelles soufflées sous les tons de la série basse. La chute trop rapide du caractère soufflé, comme en maleng, donne une sorte de système érodé à deux tons.
tone_statements.translation: Sach/Ruc and Thavung have a four-tone system with breathy vowels under the tones of the low series. Too rapid a loss of the breathy quality, as in Maleng, gives a kind of eroded two-tone system.
tone_statements.n_tones: 4 (two high-series, two low-series with breathy vowels)

tone_statements.citation: Hayes, La Vaughn H. 1983 [year per the DataCite DOI record; the sealang MKS index and the PDF page footer give 1984, as the row has it]. The register systems of Thavung. Mon-Khmer Studies 12: 91-122. doi:10.15144/mksj-12.91
tone_statements.quote: The prosodic system of Thavung consists of tone and voice register subsystems. The tone subsystem The tone subsystem is a level-pitch register system. Its four tonemes have a two-way contrast. As shown in Figure 1, pitch height distinguishes two registers, each containing two tonemes. By definition, pitch contour is nonglided. A glottal feature distinguishes between clear and glottal tones within each register. The glottal tones are enunciated with laryngeal constriction occurring near the end of the nucleic vowel. Figure 1. The Thavung Tones Register Clear Glottal High /v¹/ /v³/ Low /v²/ /v⁴/
tone_statements.summary: Four level tonemes: high/low pitch register x clear/glottal (laryngeal constriction); tone only on the main syllable, presyllable atonal (p.95); data from Ferlus's lexicon; no statement on stress.

audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant, final stress (final stress on the main syllable of sesquisyllabic/disyllabic and trisyllabic words) rests on Suwilai 1996 MKS 26 p.166. We held no copy; I downloaded the open sealang PDF, scanned pp.165-167, and found the quotation verbatim at the stated page, with the trisyllabic template also final-stressed. I also downloaded the second Glottolog phonology (Waiyanont 1998 Mahidol MA, Lao variety, open on sealang's Mahidol archive) and scanned its stress chapter: it independently states strong stress on the last syllable of di- and trisyllabic words, stress predictable, adding only a weak-stress grade on closed presyllables (no bearing on primary-stress position). sources.quote: p.75: 'The strong stress falls on the monosyllabic word and on the last position of disyllabic word and trisyllabic word. The unstress occur before the last syllable of the word.' p.76-77: three levels — strong stress always on the major (final) syllable; weak stress on closed presyllables; open presyllables unstressed; 'Stress in the Samhing Thavung is predictable'. p.79: trisyllabic [CVC.CV.'CV], strong stress on the third syllable.
